[0] everyday_reading (E): Everyday reading: the computer understands what you meant and will complain if the program is wrong. Java rule: a program with a logic error compiles and runs without any message and does exactly what the code says, which differs from what was intended.
[1] misconception (M) -> CompilesMeansWorks: wrong rule: Code that compiles is code that works. Right rule: Code that compiles and runs can still compute the wrong result (a logic error).
[2] inconsistent_trace (T) -> CompilesMeansWorks: Applies the 'computer does exactly what is written' rule unevenly: traces some lines literally but reads the intended meaning into the faulty line, and so does not see the bug. (here mixing in: "Code that compiles is code that works")

[0] names_the_element (N): A logic error is an error that makes a program do something other than what the programmer intended, without any compiler or run-time message.
[1] states_the_rule (S): If a program has a logic error, it will compile and run without generating error messages, but it will not do the right thing; the compiler and JVM cannot detect it since they don't know what the right thing is.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): Execution proceeds normally, statement by statement; the faulty statement executes without complaint and passes a wrong value or output onward.
[1] output_prediction (OP): Result is a normal-looking but wrong output, e.g. println("Hello, "); println("World!"); prints two lines where one was intended.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): Each step makes a legal state change (e.g. an empty statement after if, or resetting sum each pass), but not the intended one.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): A logic error is seen only by running the program and comparing its output with the intended output.
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): A run-time error stops the program with an exception; a logic error lets it finish with wrong output.
[2] relation_to_neighbour (R): Debugging is mostly the search for logic errors, which give wrong output without any message.
[3] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Purpose (of the category): name the errors that only testing against the intended behaviour can find, so they are found by tracing, test cases and added print statements.

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> CompilesMeansWorks: A logic error survives recompiling and rerunning unchanged; changing input may hide or reveal it; fixing it changes output only on the inputs it affected.
[1] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: A ; right after if (...) is an empty statement that forms the whole if body. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: if (x > 0); System.out.println("positive"); prints for every x
[2] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: The accumulator must be declared and initialized before the loop. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: int sum = 0; written inside the loop body: sum is reset each pass (and is out of scope after the loop)
[3] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Suspect a logic error when the program compiles and runs to the end but the output is wrong for some inputs; locate it by hand tracing, minimal test cases and print statements, since tools give no message.
[4] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: A while loop tests its condition before the first pass. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: values set before the loop already make the condition false, so the body never runs
[5] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: print vs println decides line breaks. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: println used where print was meant (or the reverse)

A run-time error stops the program with an exception; a logical error lets it finish with wrong output.
A ; right after an if or loop header is an empty statement, so the header controls nothing and the next line always runs: the program compiles but computes the wrong result.
Debugging is mostly the search for logic errors, which give wrong output without any message.
A logical error is seen only by running the program and comparing its output with the intended output.
